video_notes.title: Fine-Tuning a Model: The Easiest Way to Start (Unsloth Tutorial)
video_notes.contributed: A full hands-on walkthrough of the fine-tuning loop in Unsloth's no-code UI: baseline eval before training, LoRA/QLoRA hyperparameter choices, a real max-steps-vs-epochs mistake and its loss-chart symptom, before/after scoring, GGUF export, and calling the exported model from an external Python app.

video_notes.title: The Honest Guide To Fine-Tuning Local AI In 2026
video_notes.contributed: The decision framework for when to fine-tune versus prompt/RAG/agentic loops, the five-step pipeline (data collection, dataset engineering, LoRA training, evaluation, GGUF export), concrete token/VRAM/time benchmarks, and a hardware verdict across Nvidia, AMD, and Apple Silicon for local fine-tuning.

video_notes.title: GenAI in Production: How RAG & AI Agents Are Shaping the Future
video_notes.contributed: Mostly a RAG/agents production podcast, but it adds the 'garbage in, garbage out' warning specific to fine-tuned models inheriting training-data errors, plus general production practices (golden datasets, canary/blue-green rollouts, drift monitoring, feedback loops) that apply once a fine-tuned model ships.

video_notes.title: Learn Design Systems: Figma Variables, Components, AI, and More
video_notes.contributed: No content on model/LLM fine-tuning — this is a 4-hour Figma design-systems tutorial (design tokens, variables, components) that only uses 'AI' and 'training' in the generic design-tooling sense. It does not support any claim for this guide's topic; flagged as a cluster-assignment mismatch rather than a source.

claims.claim: Treat fine-tuning as one step inside a larger loop: pick a base model, choose one narrow behavior, build examples, baseline-test the untrained model, train, re-run the same evaluation, and only then export/ship.
claims.quote: You start with a general purpose model.

claims.claim: LoRA freezes the base model's weights and trains a small adapter on top, so fine-tuning steers existing capability toward a target behavior rather than teaching new facts.
claims.quote: the base stays frozen We train a relatively small adapter

claims.claim: Design your first fine-tuning task so the output is machine-scorable (e.g., force a JSON object with fixed fields) instead of a subjective 'does this feel nicer' judgment.
claims.quote: exactly one JSON object containing three fields, Category, severity and next action

claims.claim: Define the exact behavior you want to measure (categories, severity levels, labels) before opening any fine-tuning tool.
claims.quote: start with the behavior you want to measure and then move from there

claims.claim: Structure each training example as a system/user/assistant chat triplet; the assistant message is the exact training target the model learns to reproduce.
claims.quote: the assistant message contains the correct answer

claims.claim: Run the identical evaluation (same questions, scoring rules, and generation settings) on the base model before and after fine-tuning, or the before/after comparison is meaningless.
claims.quote: same evaluation, same questions, same scoring rules, comparable generation settings

claims.claim: Score a structured-output fine-tune on multiple axes at once: correct category, correct severity, valid JSON, exact required keys, and usefulness of the free-text field.
claims.quote: did it return a valid JSON, did it use the exact required keys

claims.claim: Keep three separate data splits: training data updates the adapter, validation data checks generalization while you iterate, and a final test set stays completely untouched until you need to verify what survived your decisions.
claims.quote: keep a final test set completely untouched as well

claims.claim: Full fine-tuning updates every model parameter and is expensive; LoRA instead trains only a small extra set of parameters while the base model stays frozen.
claims.quote: Lora is a fine tuning method that lets you adapt a large language model by training only a small extra set of parameters

claims.claim: QLoRA compresses the frozen base model to 4-bit precision while still training a small trainable LoRA adapter on top, which is why the experiment can run comfortably on a normal machine.
claims.quote: the Bayes model is compressed often to four bits

claims.claim: Pick a deliberately small base model (Qwen 2.5 0.5B) for a first fine-tune since the goal is to learn the loop, not to ship a production financial model.
claims.quote: I'm going to be using Queen 2.505 B

claims.claim: Unsloth has a built-in recipe builder to auto-generate datasets, but the presenter prefers hand-building datasets (e.g., via ChatGPT) depending on the task.
claims.quote: I usually prefer getting my own data sets essentially just going to charge PT and having it create a data set for me

claims.claim: For the tutorial run: 4-bit quantization, LoRA/QLoRA method, 3 epochs, 512-token context length, batch size 2, rank 16, adapter scale (alpha) 1.0, dropout 0, and gradient accumulation over 4 batches.
claims.quote: We're going to be setting the low rank at 16

claims.claim: Dropout randomly ignores some training signals to reduce overfitting; the tutorial leaves it at zero so nothing is dropped during this small experimental run.
claims.quote: dropout randomly ignores some training signals to reduce overfitting

claims.claim: Gradient accumulation collects gradients across several mini-batches before applying one update, letting you simulate a larger batch size without using more memory.
claims.quote: the model collects gradients from four batches, making one update

claims.claim: A physical batch size of 2 with gradient accumulation of 4 means the optimizer effectively sees eight examples before applying one full update.
claims.quote: effectively sees eight examples before one full update

claims.claim: Focus first on three settings — epochs, learning rate, and rank — since rank controls how much capacity the adapter has to learn, and more capacity is not automatically better.
claims.quote: Three parameters I want you to recognize immediately are epochs, learning rate and rank

claims.claim: A higher LoRA rank gives the adapter more capacity to learn new patterns, but costs more memory and parameters.
claims.quote: the rank controls roughly how much capacity the adapter has

claims.claim: Setting 'max steps' to 3 instead of 3 epochs is a critical configuration mistake: it makes the optimizer update the model only three times total instead of cycling through the whole dataset three times.
claims.quote: I mistakenly set these Max steps at 3

claims.claim: A training loss chart trending upward instead of downward is a visible symptom that something in the run configuration is wrong, not a normal training artifact.
claims.quote: the training loss chart is trending upwards instead of training downwards

claims.claim: After switching from max-steps=3 to epochs=3, training loss visibly trended downward, confirming the earlier config was the cause of the broken run.
claims.quote: the training loss is gradually going down

claims.claim: On the tutorial's finance-triage classifier, the fine-tuned model scored 75 composite versus 74 for the base model, and correctly classified 12 of 25 test cases versus 11 for the base model — a real but small improvement from one iteration.
claims.quote: the composite result shows us that the fine tune model performed has a score of 75 whereas the base model has a score of 74

claims.theme: fine-tuning is a loop, not an event
claims.claim: Fine-tuning is not a single event but an experimental loop: train, evaluate, inspect failures, change one thing, retrain, and repeat until results are acceptable.
claims.quote: fine tuning is not an event, it's essentially an experimental loop

claims.theme: change one variable at a time
claims.claim: Between iterations, change exactly one thing — either how the data is specified or one configuration parameter — so you can attribute any change in results to that one change.
claims.quote: Then what we do is we go back, we change one thing

claims.claim: Export the finished fine-tune to GGUF format, which is optimized for local inference, rather than keeping it only inside the training tool.
claims.quote: we're going to be exporting the model using the file formats gguf

claims.claim: Use the Q4_K_M quantization level at export time (distinct from the 4-bit quantization used during training) as the recommended balance of size and quality for local inference.
claims.quote: we're going to be selecting the Q4KM

claims.claim: After exporting, point the model hub to the local export folder rather than re-downloading the model, since the files already exist on disk.
claims.quote: we are not downloading the model again

claims.claim: Unsloth exposes an OpenAI-compatible API locally, so an external Python app can call the fine-tuned model with the standard OpenAI client pointed at localhost, reusing the same system prompt used during training.
claims.quote: OnSlot provides an OpenAI compatible API locally

claims.theme: fine-tuning is not the whole system
claims.claim: Fine-tuning only changes a model's behavior; a real production system around it still needs context, evaluation, application logic, callable tools, and guardrails.
claims.quote: fine tuning only changes the behavior of the model

claims.claim: A first fine-tuning dataset can be as small as 20 to 50 examples, or a few hundred, plus a separate evaluation dataset — don't start with thousands of examples.
claims.quote: The data set could be 20 to 50 or a few hundred examples

claims.theme: fine-tuning implements persona, not just prompting
claims.claim: A system prompt can't cover every type of question a model will face, but fine-tuning can bake a persistent persona or style directly into the model's weights so it shows up consistently across unseen questions.
claims.quote: your system prompt is not going to cover every type of question that you might throw at a model

claims.theme: LoRA touches a small fraction of parameters
claims.claim: Fine-tuning with a LoRA adapter typically only needs to train about half a percent to 2% of a model's parameters, not the full weight set.
claims.quote: it's enough to train, say, half to 2% of the parameters of the model

claims.claim: Many AI platforms that claim to 'train on your data' are actually just injecting information into a prompt rather than fine-tuning the model.
claims.quote: a lot of them just inject your information into a prompt

claims.claim: Use a four-step flowchart before fine-tuning: try a better prompt first, then add RAG if that fails, then consider an agentic loop if that fails, and only fine-tune if all three fail.
claims.quote: First, you can just try a better prompt and evaluate whether the model performs well enough on a task.

claims.claim: Fine-tuning is the right tool when you need a guaranteed consistent style/persona every time, or when you want to bake static, rarely-changing knowledge directly into the model (reserving RAG only for the parts that change).
claims.quote: create a model that writes like you every time with a real guarantee

claims.claim: Fine-tuning will cost at least a weekend of iteration and requires a pretty competent GPU, unlike prompting or RAG.
claims.quote: It will cost you at least a weekend of screwing around

claims.claim: A first fine-tuning project has roughly five steps: data collection, dataset engineering, LoRA training, evaluation, and GGUF export.
claims.quote: for your first fine-tuning project, there's roughly five steps

claims.claim: Fine-tuning an 8B-parameter model may require on the order of one to two million-plus tokens of raw data before any transformation into training pairs.
claims.quote: you might need a million, 2 million plus tokens of raw data

claims.claim: A language model cannot self-correct bad training data; feeding it uncleaned, error-ridden data makes the fine-tuned result worse, not neutral.
claims.quote: if you feed it bad data, then actually you're going to make the end result much worse

claims.theme: turning raw text into training pairs
claims.claim: To fine-tune on raw source material like transcripts, use a local LLM to synthesize a relevant question for each text snippet, then pair it with the matching answer, converting raw text into chat-format prompt/response pairs.
claims.quote: use a local language model to generate a question that is relevant for that little text snippet

claims.claim: Because LoRA only retrains a small fraction of parameters, a run that might take 20 hours with full fine-tuning can finish in about 2 hours, enabling fast iterate-and-fix cycles.
claims.quote: instead of having to wait 20 hours to get a result, maybe you can get some fine tuning done in just 2 hours

claims.claim: Fine-tuning a medium-sized language model took roughly 2 to 3 hours on an RTX 5090 in the presenter's home-lab tests.
claims.quote: it would take something like 2 to 3 hours on a 5090

claims.claim: A 27-billion-parameter model will likely exceed 14GB of VRAM to fine-tune even with an efficient quantized version.
claims.quote: a 27 billion parameter model likely will exceed 14 GB

claims.claim: Offloading fine-tuning parameters to regular system RAM instead of dedicated GPU VRAM will grind fine-tuning to a halt, and sometimes doesn't work at all.
claims.quote: this will grind fine-tuning to a halt and sometimes that just doesn't work at all

claims.theme: AMD as a middle-ground GPU option
claims.claim: AMD is actively building CUDA counterparts (ROCm) and you can already fine-tune a lot of models on it, making a recent AMD GPU a viable middle-ground option versus paying the 'Nvidia tax', though compatibility varies.
claims.quote: AMD is actively developing CUDA counterparts. With Rockom, you can actually fine-tune quite a lot of models already

claims.claim: Avoid fine-tuning on Apple Silicon: most models lack MLX ports, and even when available, fine-tuning on Apple Silicon is much slower than on a good Nvidia GPU.
claims.quote: What I would definitely avoid is to fine-tune on Apple silicon

claims.claim: Write proper tests comparing the fine-tuned model against the untrained vanilla model to figure out whether a problem lies in the LoRA training step or the dataset engineering step.
claims.quote: write some proper tests to figure out whether your finetude model is actually performing better than the vanilla model

claims.claim: GGUF export makes a fine-tuned model easy to run in consumer-friendly local tools like LM Studio and Ollama.
claims.quote: format of a model that's easier to run on platforms like LM Studio and Olama

claims.claim: If you fine-tune a model on the same messy or biased source data that would poison a RAG system, the fine-tuned model inherits whatever errors or biases lurk in that training data.
claims.quote: the fine-tuned models usually inherit whatever errors or biases lurk in the training data

claims.claim: Use golden datasets and manual review during development, run full end-to-end tests with adversarial edge cases in staging, and keep A/B testing and re-evaluating after deployment — testing is a continuous cycle, not a one-time certification.
claims.quote: use golden data sets and manual uh reviews to assess uh output quality

claims.claim: Manage model or data-source updates with versioning and safe rollout patterns like blue-green or canary deployments, validating before switching traffic over.
claims.quote: we rely on versioning and safe rollout patterns like uh blue green uh deployments or canary deployments

claims.claim: Build in explicit feedback mechanisms like thumbs up/down and comments so users can add context that helps refine model responses over time.
claims.quote: thumbs up, thumbs down, comments

claims.claim: Key risks to actively mitigate when an LLM app goes to production include hallucinations, data leaks, bias, prompt injection, IP concerns, and runaway usage costs.
claims.quote: hallucinations data leaks um and bias prompt injections are a big one

disagreements.topic: Where fine-tuning sits relative to prompting, RAG, and agents

positions.position: Fine-tuning should be the last resort in a strict escalation: try a better prompt, then RAG, then an agentic loop, and only fine-tune if all three fail, because fine-tuning costs at least a weekend and a competent GPU.

Frames fine-tuning as carrying its own distinct data-quality risk ('garbage in, garbage out' applies to fine-tuned models inheriting bad training data) rather than ranking it strictly below RAG — the emphasis is on data cleanliness as the gate, not sequencing fine-tuning last.

gaps: No guidance on choosing LoRA rank/alpha for a real production-sized task — only one toy example (rank 16, alpha 1.0) is shown, with no rule of thumb for scaling up.
No coverage of cloud or managed fine-tuning services (pricing, turnaround, scaling) — both detailed tutorials assume a local/home-lab GPU.
No comparison between Unsloth and other fine-tuning frameworks (e.g., Axolotl, Hugging Face PEFT/TRL) or criteria for choosing among them.
No discussion of merging multiple LoRA adapters, swapping adapters at inference time, or deciding when to merge an adapter into the base weights versus keeping it separate.
AMD ROCm and Apple Silicon/MLX fine-tuning performance are described qualitatively ('your mileage might vary') with no actual benchmark numbers.
No treatment of full-parameter fine-tuning trade-offs, or alignment-style fine-tuning (RLHF/DPO) as an alternative to supervised LoRA fine-tuning.
No discussion of licensing or IP implications of exporting and redistributing a fine-tuned open-weight model.

The design-systems video in this cluster (lsgVRCJ4fko) does not address LLM fine-tuning at all, so this cluster has no material on integrating fine-tuned models into design/product tooling workflows despite nominally being grouped together.
